newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebel chief seen as image conscious union type.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel chief seen as image conscious union type.

text.p: With Peru's hostage crisis well into its fourth week, a picture is emerging of the man who led the Marxist rebel attack on the Japanese ambassador's home as an image-conscious, intelligent and audacious guerrilla leader.

Government sources said Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the former textile worker who still holds 74 VIP hostages inside the residence, is obsessed with his image and wants to present himself as a strong leader who is also generous and humane.
"For every three steps forward he can take four back. He has a highly complex mentality," a senior Peruvian official told Reuters.

Since storming the diplomatic mansion on Dec. 17 with a band of about 15 well-armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, Cerpa has seized every opportunity to bask in the media attention the hostage crisis has attracted.

At an impromptu news conference held inside the residence on New Year's Eve, the portly rebel leader, his face partly hidden behind a red and white neckerchief, regaled journalists with a 40-minute critique of Peru's government.
"At first he was very aggressive but he has calmed down a lot," the government source said.
In the first hours of the siege, Cerpa freed all the women who attended the ill-fated party. Further "goodwill gestures" of hostage releases followed.
"He has tried to appear generous but obviously (the hostages) were of little use to him," the government source said.

The MRTA leader has clung on to those captives he considers the best bargaining chips in talks with the government, including top government and security officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats and President Alberto Fujimori's brother, Pedro.
Cerpa has fiercely rejected the "terrorist" tag the Peruvian government has given to the MRTA and has been at pains to stress that hostages were not being mistreated.
Former hostages recount how the 43-year-old guerrilla would circulate around the two-floor mansion explaining the roots of the MRTA and engaging in ideological debates.

"He explained his strategy and what his movement wanted ... My personal opinion is that he is a cultured man, well-read and quite intelligent," said Carlos Aquino Rodriguez, a university professor who was held for five days.
Others who have met the rebel leader describe him as thoughtful and soft-spoken. "He looked like a university type," one said.
In a radio conversation with Education Minister Domingo Palermo that was witnessed by foreign correspondents on Friday, Cerpa spoke deferentially and showed a sense of humour.
Asked by Palermo if he was available for a weekend meeting at the residence Cerpa quipped: "Here we are and we're not going anywhere."

Cerpa, the only MRTA leader still at large, has treated negotiations to end the siege rather as a union leader would approach a pay dispute, the government source said. "He's like someone who goes to see his boss asking for a raise of $100 but knowing he will only receive $50 or less," he said.
Until the Dec. 17 attack, Cerpa lived in the shadow of more notorious MRTA leaders such as Victor Polay, now in jail.
Cerpa's political activities began when he joined a group of union leaders organising workers at the Cromotex textile factory near Lima in 1977.
He was arrested and held in jail for 10 months and on his release went underground and started to help organise the MRTA.
A string of attacks followed on targets ranging from a fast food outlet to a Catholic church. He also led or took part in attacks on a luxury hotel, a top restaurant and a newspaper.
The mother of Cerpa's two young sons is one of the 400 jailed MRTA prisoners he has demanded be freed in exchange for the remaining hostages inside the diplomaic residence.
His mother, Felicita Cartolini, who looks after his boys in France, said her now famous son was not unusually dangerous.
"I know the human side of my son and I believe he will respect all of the hostages...I don't think he is violent at the moment," she said.
